questions.title: Does a spouse's consent to a home entry waive the other spouse's Fourth Amendment rights?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the third-party consent rule mentioned in this case. The court cites United States v. Cellitti, stating that a third party can give consent to search a place where both they and the defendant have a legitimate expectation of privacy. In this case, Lisa consented, but Jaison was the one charged. Does this mean that as long as a spouse lives there, they can essentially 'sign away' the other spouse's privacy rights regardless of the other spouse's wishes?

questions.title: How does the 'totality of the circumstances' test handle suggestive language like 'we need to come inside'?
questions.question_body: The defendant argued that Officer Kizer coerced consent by saying, 'I’m sensing that we almost need to come inside.' To me, that sounds like a demand rather than a request. However, the court says the district court didn't err in finding the consent voluntary based on the 'totality of the circumstances.' What other factors in the 'totality' usually outweigh a specific phrase that sounds coercive?

questions.title: What constitutes the 'scope of consent' when police enter a home for a welfare check?
questions.question_body: The police entered the home specifically to check on the welfare of children. Once inside, they conducted a 'quick canvas' of the home and located the husband in a separate bedroom. I'm struggling with the 'objective reasonableness' standard here: would a reasonable person who allows police in to check on kids also assume the police are allowed to search other bedrooms for an adult?

questions.title: What is the 'clear error' standard of review for findings of voluntary consent?
questions.question_body: The court mentions that its role is limited because it reviews the district court's finding of voluntary consent for 'clear error.' I'm a bit confused about the procedural difference here. Is the appellate court performing a brand new analysis of the body camera footage, or are they only intervening if the district court's conclusion was completely irrational?

questions.title: Does an initial refusal of consent make a subsequent agreement more likely to be viewed as coerced?
questions.question_body: In the facts, Lisa explicitly said, 'I’d prefer you not' when first asked to let the officer in. Then, after some time passed and the officer asked again, she said 'Okay.' Does the fact that she initially refused create a stronger presumption of coercion for the second request, or does the court view the second 'Okay' as a conscious change of mind that reinforces voluntariness?

questions.title: Why would a court decline to rule on 'exigent circumstances' if voluntary consent is already established?
questions.question_body: At the end of the opinion, the court says it doesn't need to consider the government's alternative arguments regarding 'exigent circumstances' and 'inevitable discovery' because the consent was valid. I don't understand the strategic or legal reason for this. If the government has three different legal justifications for the entry, why wouldn't the court rule on all of them to make the precedent stronger?
